statement:
The point $P$ has coordinates $(x,y)$ with respect to the origin $O$. By writing $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$, or otherwise, show that, if the line $OP$ is rotated by $60^\circ$ clockwise about $O$, the new $y$-coordinate of $P$ is $\tfrac12(y-\sqrt3\,x)$.

What is the new $y$-coordinate in the case of an anti-clockwise rotation by $60^\circ$?

An equilateral triangle $OBC$ has vertices at $O$, $(1,0)$ and $(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\sqrt3)$. The point $P$ has coordinates $(x,y)$. The perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line through $C$ and $O$ is $h_1$; the perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line through $O$ and $B$ is $h_2$; and the perpendicular distance from $P$ to the line through $B$ and $C$ is $h_3$.

Show that $h_1=\tfrac12|y-\sqrt3\,x|$ and find expressions for $h_2$ and $h_3$.

Show that $h_1+h_2+h_3=\tfrac12\sqrt3$ if and only if $P$ lies on or in the triangle $OBC$.
solution:
**Rotation.** Write $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$. A clockwise rotation by $60^\circ$ changes $\theta$ to $\theta-\pi/3$, so the new $y$-coordinate is
$$r\sin(\theta-\tfrac\pi3)=r\left(\sin\theta\cos\tfrac\pi3-\cos\theta\sin\tfrac\pi3\right)=\frac12y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}x=\frac12(y-\sqrt3\,x).$$
For an anti-clockwise rotation, $\theta\to\theta+\pi/3$, giving $\tfrac12(y+\sqrt3\,x)$.

**Distances.** The line $OC$ passes through $(0,0)$ and $(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$, so it has equation $y=\sqrt3\,x$. The perpendicular distance from $P$ to this line is
$$h_1=\frac{|y-\sqrt3\,x|}{\sqrt{1+3}}=\frac12|y-\sqrt3\,x|.$$

The line $OB$ is the $x$-axis, so $h_2=|y|$.

The line $BC$ passes through $(1,0)$ and $(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$, with gradient $-\sqrt3$, so its equation is $y=-\sqrt3(x-1)$, i.e. $\sqrt3\,x+y-\sqrt3=0$. Hence
$$h_3=\frac{|\sqrt3\,x+y-\sqrt3|}{\sqrt{3+1}}=\frac12|\sqrt3\,x+y-\sqrt3|.$$

**Sum of distances (Viviani's theorem).** For a point $P$ inside (or on) the triangle, $y\ge0$ and the expressions are all non-negative with consistent signs, so the absolute values can be dropped with the correct sign and
$$h_1+h_2+h_3=\frac12(\sqrt3\,x-y)+y+\frac12(\sqrt3-\sqrt3\,x-y)=\frac12\sqrt3,$$
(using the orientations appropriate to the interior). For points outside the triangle, one or more of the signed terms change sign, so the sum exceeds $\tfrac12\sqrt3$. Hence the sum equals $\tfrac12\sqrt3$ exactly when $P$ lies on or inside the triangle $OBC$ (this constant value is the altitude of the equilateral triangle).
hints: For the rotation, use y = r sin θ and the sine subtraction formula.
Each h_i is the distance to a side; use the perpendicular-distance formula.
Viviani: the sum of distances to the three sides of an equilateral triangle equals its altitude.
